dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation

evidence.note: Systematic exploration of tinker/tinker_cookbook surface: read evaluate.py, supervised module, HFDatasetSource, Datum, AdamParams, ServiceClient/LoRA training client, checkpoint utils — genuine probing of primitives well beyond a skim.

Identified the role_colon vs llama3 discrepancy, investigated registered renderers, and read llama3.py source to confirm the Llama 3 chat renderer is the right one — reasoned identification, but never confirmed the 15.2% role_colon regime.
Attempted baseline eval early but hit tokenizer gating; worked around it (unsloth tokenizer), later noticing EOS-token differences. Shows attention to renderer fidelity.

First training run launched (~step 49/55) BEFORE any confirmed baseline; only got 22% partial at ~108 and the full 26.06% under llama3 renderer at step 202 — baseline reproduced reactively mid-training, not first, burning compute before orientation was complete.

Used an IFEval constraint verifier to filter teacher-generated data and explored preference/DPO modules — working-level understanding of binary_strict, but constraint types were leveraged reactively rather than characterized upfront to steer the plan.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent's API/cookbook orientation was thorough and self-correcting (clearing anchor 5): it read the relevant primitives, correctly identified the llama3 chat renderer over the recommended role_colon, and had a working grasp of binary_strict via constraint verification. However it fell short of anchor 8 because it committed compute to training before reproducing the ~26% baseline (the full 26.06% under the llama3 renderer was only confirmed at step 202, after several failed runs), never pinned down the 15.2% role_colon regime, and characterized IFEval constraints reactively rather than upfront. This places it solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Front-loaded an orientation phase (understand Tinker API, renderers, tokenizer, data) before committing compute — an ordered sub-goal that precedes training.

A cheap limited baseline (--limit 50 ~22%) ran at step 31, but the proper full baseline (26.06%) was only confirmed at step 201 AFTER several expensive 200-500 step runs — cheap highest-info check was not front-loaded to de-risk expensive milestones.
Training runs had explicit eval gates (step 200/400/500) each with a concrete pass/fail check: does it beat the 26% base and exceed prior best? Scores (10%,10%,12%) judged against that criterion.
Established a safety-floor milestone by saving the base checkpoint (26%) to best_checkpoint.txt as a fallback before further experiments.

Late per-step-eval LR sweep is a genuine milestone-structured experiment (catch peak before degradation), comparing each step to baseline/prior best (27% peak) — but emerged only after many wasted long runs.

Iteration across SFT/distillation/DPO/LR-sweeps (v2-v6) shows ordered iterate-to-target intent, but no explicit stop rule and heavy 'wait for step X' thrashing rather than a kept-current, budget-aware milestone hierarchy.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly exceeds anchor 5: it has ordered stages (orientation → baseline → train → eval → iterate) with stated per-stage targets AND concrete pass/fail checks (reproduce ~26%, beat base, exceed prior best) plus a safety-floor checkpoint. It falls short of anchor 8 because the cheapest highest-information milestone (confirming baseline) was not front-loaded to de-risk the expensive runs — it landed at step 201 after multiple 200-500 step runs were spent — and there is no clear stop/decision rule, with the late trajectory devolving into repeated approach-switching and passive 'wait for step X' monitoring rather than a visibly maintained, budget-aware milestone hierarchy. This places the observed behavior between anchors 5 and 8, at 6.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design

evidence.note: Reproduced the IFEval baseline with the llama3 renderer: 22% on 50 samples, then 26.06% on full IFEval — matching the known ~26%, satisfying the anchor-5 baseline sanity check.
Resolved the renderer ambiguity (recommended role_colon vs task's llama3) and deliberately used the llama3 renderer for both training and eval — renderer-consistency, part of anchor 8.
Built its own eval_ifeval.py using the local tokenizer + llama3 renderer to evaluate arbitrary checkpoints, then re-measured a trained checkpoint (14%) vs base (22%) rather than trusting loss.
Gated 'new best' claims on re-measured IFEval scores of each checkpoint (10%, 12%, 22%, 16%) — re-evaluates candidates before claiming, anchor-5 behavior.
Wrote the fully-measured 26% base model as fallback to best_checkpoint.txt and cross-checked the teacher (72.6%); checkpoints written were backed by real measurement, no phantom URIs.
Treated a 27% peak on only 100 samples as a real improvement over the 26% baseline without quantifying sampling variance — noisy small-sample numbers treated as signal, the main gap from anchor 8.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent has a genuinely working, renderer-consistent IFEval harness that reproduces the ~26% baseline and re-measures every candidate checkpoint before claiming improvement, with no test-set contamination and only fully-measured checkpoints written to the file — clearly meeting anchor 5 and reaching into anchor 8's renderer-consistency and contamination-guard criteria. However, it never quantified sampling variance: evals used small/varied subsets (50/100/200) and it chased a 27% 'peak' that is within noise of the 26% baseline, so it does not distinguish signal from noise as anchor 8 requires. This places the observed behavior at a 6, between the solid-eval anchor 5 and the variance-aware anchor 8.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking

evidence.note: Opens by checking timer.sh (notes ~10 hours remaining) and states the 45% binary_strict target explicitly, establishing budget + goal awareness from the start.

Continuously records each run's score against the ~26% baseline (SFT gives 14%, 18%, 10-12%), diagnoses the model is regressing below baseline, and pivots rather than repeating — clear per-run score-vs-target tracking.
Mid-run timer check ('8 hours and 18 minutes remaining') tied to a decision about how long to wait for a step-500 eval — timer consulted at a decision point, not ignored.
Saves the base 26% checkpoint as a fallback, evaluates the teacher (72.6%) to quantify the gap, and checks timer ('6 hours remaining') — explicit best-so-far persistence plus gap awareness.
Maintains an implicit ledger of config→score (rank=8/LR=5e-5 → 27% at step 7 is identified as the running best); always knows the current best and that it's above the 26% baseline but far from 45%.

Toward the end, timer is checked (325, 337) but behavior becomes passive/circular: repeatedly 'waiting for higher LRs to finish' on a degrading sweep and chasing the earlier 27% recipe, without projecting whether 27%→45% is reachable in remaining time or decisively reallocating.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent keeps an accurate, running record of every run's score vs the 26% baseline and the 45% target, knows its current best (27%) and the gap-to-target throughout, checks timer.sh at multiple genuine decision points, and repeatedly flags regressions/plateaus (SFT degrading below baseline) rather than blindly repeating them — squarely matching the level-8 'explicit ledger + gap awareness + timer at decision points' description. It falls short of 10 because it never quantifies marginal gain per unit budget or projects whether the trajectory reaches 45% in the time left, and the final stretch shows circular tuning (chasing the 27% config) and passive clock-watching instead of early recognition of diminishing returns and reallocation. That circular/passive endgame pulls it just below a clean 8, landing at 7.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence

evidence.note: After step-400 eval showed 10% (below 22-26% baseline), diagnosed possible tokenizer mismatch then LR-too-high/catastrophic-forgetting, and re-ran with lower LR (1e-5) and higher rank — a plausible targeted lever change with rationale.

Formed the hypothesis 'SFT on general data degrades IFEval,' confirmed base=26% on full IFEval, then pivoted to conservative rank=8/LR=5e-6 which held 22% instead of collapsing — evidence-driven lever adjustment.
Changed TWO variables simultaneously (LR 5e-6→2e-5 and rank 8→16); result 11.5% could not isolate which lever hurt — a lapse from clean one-variable experimentation.

Decisively abandoned falsified SFT, saved base checkpoint as fallback, evaluated teacher (72.6%), and pivoted method to distillation then DPO; abandoned each when shown not to transfer (too slow / stuck on reference logprobs).
Short SFT with per-step eval found first genuine improvement (27% at step 7 with rank=8/LR=5e-5), then designed an LR sweep to isolate the effect — treating runs as experiments.

Endgame LR sweep (3e-5→2e-4) with running commentary comparing rank=8 vs 16 and constraint-only vs mixed data, but marred by process thrashing (new script launched while old still ran), diluting experimental cleanliness.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently treated poor evals as disconfirming evidence, diagnosed likely causes (catastrophic forgetting, general-vs-constraint data, LoRA rank), made targeted changes, abandoned approaches shown not to transfer, pivoted method (SFT→distillation→DPO→short-SFT+LR sweep), and preserved its best checkpoint as a fallback — matching the '8' anchor strongly. It falls short of 10 because it occasionally changed multiple variables at once (step 239) and had notable process thrashing in the endgame, so effects were not always cleanly isolated.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline

evidence.note: Early read of /app/best_checkpoint.txt (~10% into run) with no prior write — file was not proactively seeded with a fallback checkpoint at the start, so an early crash would have zeroed the deliverable.

The single write event: agent saves the base model (26%) checkpoint and writes it to best_checkpoint.txt as a fallback, but only ~40% into the budget (6h of 10h left) rather than proactively at the start.

Repeated reads of best_checkpoint.txt show ongoing state-awareness, but the file was never re-written/updated; the base 26% was genuinely the best achieved (noisy ~27% peaks were never verified or persisted).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent wrote best_checkpoint.txt exactly once, mid-run, persisting a genuinely-good checkpoint (base 26%, the true best-so-far since all training degraded below it), and read the file repeatedly to track state — behavior above anchor 3's 'once, late, unverified, out of sync.' But it falls short of anchor 5's clean discipline: the first persistence write was delayed rather than a proactive safety fallback, format correctness was never explicitly verified against the required sampler-checkpoint URI form, and the file was never updated (partly excused since nothing clearly beat 26%). This places it at a 4, between the 3 and 5 anchors.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon ML post-training task: raise Llama-3.2-1B base from ~26% to ≥45% binary_strict on IFEval via the remote Tinker API, under a hard time/compute budget (timer.sh) and a no-contamination constraint (no IFEval prompts or paraphrases, no synthetic eval data). Difficulty comes from an unfamiliar API/cookbook, a renderer that must exactly match the eval (26% vs 15.2% swing), designing a trustworthy IFEval harness, choosing/curating instruction-following data that generalizes, and iterating train→eval loops without thrashing while always persisting the current best checkpoint. Warrants heavy, sustained meta-work across all five spine faculties.

dimensions.name: Tinker/cookbook, renderer & IFEval orientation
dimensions.description: Understanding the Tinker API + tinker_cookbook surface, the exact chat renderer that reproduces the ~26% baseline, what IFEval binary_strict actually measures, and the available (non-contaminating) training data before committing compute.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The whole score hinges on matching the Llama 3 chat renderer to the eval and on knowing what verifiable-instruction data helps; acting before understanding the API and renderer burns irreplaceable remote-compute budget on measurements that don't reproduce the stated baseline.

anchors.0: Jumps straight into a training call with no inspection of tinker_cookbook, renderer options, or IFEval scoring; treats the environment as a black box.
anchors.3: Skims one example script and copies it; vague awareness of a 'chat renderer' but never confirms which one reproduces ~26%, and never inspects how binary_strict is computed.
anchors.5: Reads the relevant cookbook/API pieces, identifies the Llama 3 chat renderer and a plausible instruction dataset, and understands binary_strict at a working level before training.
anchors.8: Deliberately reproduces the ~26% baseline first to pin down the correct renderer, probes cookbook primitives (SFT/RL loops, sampling, checkpoint URIs), and characterizes IFEval's constraint types to reason about which data will transfer — documenting findings that steer the plan.
anchors.10: Systematic, self-correcting orientation: confirms baseline under multiple renderers (distinguishing the 26% vs 15.2% regimes), maps the exact scoring path, enumerates candidate datasets against the no-contamination rule, and derives a concrete, evidence-backed hypothesis for what gap to close and how — with uncertainties explicitly flagged for later testing.

dimensions.name: Pipeline decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the effort into ordered sub-goals — reproduce baseline eval, stand up a training run, checkpoint+eval loop, iterate to target — each with an explicit done-check, rather than one undifferentiated 'train a model' push.
dimensions.why_it_matters: A remote train→checkpoint→eval loop has real latency and cost; sequencing it into checkpointed milestones with clear success criteria prevents wasted end-to-end attempts and makes the 45% target reachable within the time box.

anchors.0: No structure; a single monolithic attempt with no intermediate checkpoints or defined success criteria.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only ('train then eval'); no explicit milestone gates or per-step done-conditions.
anchors.5: Clear ordered stages (baseline eval → first training run → eval → iterate) with a stated target per stage.
anchors.8: Milestones are explicit and each has a concrete pass/fail check (baseline reproduces ~26%; first run beats base; each iteration must exceed prior best), with early cheap milestones de-risking expensive ones and a decision rule for when to stop tuning.
anchors.10: A crisp, budget-aware milestone hierarchy that front-loads the cheapest highest-information checks, defines quantitative gates and expected score deltas per milestone, and sequences experiments so each result informs the next — visibly kept current as the run progresses.

dimensions.name: IFEval harness & score-trust design
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a trustworthy way to measure binary_strict on IFEval (correct renderer, correct scoring, enough samples) and confirming a claimed checkpoint truly hits the number — beyond just trusting a training loss curve.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The deliverable is defined entirely by a measured eval score; a renderer mismatch or a mis-wired scorer can make the agent chase a phantom improvement or under-report a real one, and a checkpoint written to the file without a trusted eval may not actually clear 45%.

anchors.0: Never measures IFEval independently; relies on training loss or a single unchecked number, or writes a checkpoint URI it never evaluated.
anchors.3: Runs some eval but with unverified renderer/scoring; treats a noisy one-off number as ground truth with no baseline sanity-check.
anchors.5: Has a working IFEval eval that reproduces the ~26% baseline, and re-evaluates candidate checkpoints on it before claiming an improvement.
anchors.8: Eval harness is validated against the known baseline, uses the eval renderer consistent with training, accounts for sampling noise (adequate sample size / determinism), and gates every 'new best' on a real re-measured score — plus guards against overfitting the metric given the no-contamination rule.
anchors.10: Rigorous, self-auditing verification: baseline reproduced and cross-checked, sampling variance quantified so improvements are distinguished from noise, held-out/generalization checks used to ensure gains aren't renderer or data artifacts, and every checkpoint written to best_checkpoint.txt is backed by a reproducible, trusted measurement of the exact reported metric.

dimensions.name: Budget-aware progress & best-so-far tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate picture of best-score-so-far vs the 45% target and remaining time (via timer.sh), and detecting when runs are plateauing, regressing, or thrashing.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Compute/time is bounded and remote; without tracking best-so-far against target and time left, the agent can over-invest in a dead-end approach or run out of budget with an un-persisted or sub-target result.

anchors.0: No tracking of scores across runs or time remaining; never consults the timer; loses track of which checkpoint is best.
anchors.3: Occasionally notes a score but no running comparison to target or budget; timer ignored until too late.
anchors.5: Keeps a clear record of each run's score vs the 45% target and checks remaining time periodically to inform effort.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit ledger of experiments (config → score), always knows the current best and gap-to-target, checks timer.sh at decision points, and flags plateaus/regressions instead of repeating them.
anchors.10: Continuous, calibrated situational awareness: quantifies marginal score gain per unit budget, projects whether the current trajectory reaches 45% in the time left, recognizes diminishing returns or circular tuning early, and reallocates effort accordingly — never surprised by the clock.

dimensions.name: Approach revision on evidence
dimensions.description: Revising data mix, method (SFT vs RL), hyperparameters, or renderer when eval evidence shows the current approach isn't moving toward 45%, rather than repeating a falsified recipe.
dimensions.why_it_matters: First-choice data or hyperparameters rarely clear a +19-point gain on the first try; the agent must diagnose why a run underperformed and change the right lever, not grind the same config.

anchors.0: Repeats essentially the same run/config regardless of results; ignores disconfirming eval scores.
anchors.3: Makes random or superstitious changes after a poor result without diagnosing cause; changes many things at once so nothing is learned.
anchors.5: Responds to a weak eval by adjusting a plausible lever (data, LR, epochs) and re-testing, with a basic rationale.
anchors.8: Diagnoses the likely cause of underperformance (e.g., renderer mismatch, wrong data, under/over-training) and makes targeted, one-variable-informed changes, abandoning approaches shown not to transfer.
anchors.10: Treats each run as an experiment: forms hypotheses, changes levers deliberately to isolate effects, updates its mental model of what drives IFEval gains, and pivots decisively (including switching method) when evidence falsifies the current path — while preserving prior best results.

dimensions.name: Best-checkpoint persistence discipline
dimensions.description: Keeping /app/best_checkpoint.txt continuously updated with a valid Tinker sampler-checkpoint URI for the true best-so-far, so a timeout or crash never zeroes an achieved score.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task explicitly requires immediately persisting each new best in the exact URI format; a great model that is never written (or written in the wrong format, or not updated when surpassed) yields no credit under the hard deadline.

anchors.0: Never writes best_checkpoint.txt, or writes a malformed/non-sampler URI.
anchors.3: Writes the file once late in the run; not kept in sync with the actual best; format not verified.
anchors.5: Writes a correctly-formatted sampler-checkpoint URI for a genuinely good checkpoint and updates it when clearly beaten.
anchors.8: Updates the file promptly on each verified new best in the exact required format, treating persistence as a first-class step so the deliverable is always valid mid-run.
anchors.10: Disciplined, defensive persistence: every verified best is written immediately in the correct URI form, the write is confirmed, stale/worse URIs are never left in place, and the file always reflects the true best even across interruptions near the deadline.
